parts.title: Part 1
script: Good morning, Clearway Driving School, Linda speaking.
Hello. I'd like to book some driving lessons.
Of course. Can I take your name?
Tomás Ruiz. The surname is R, U, I, Z.
And how old are you, Tomás?
Have you had any lessons before?
Yes, I had five lessons in my home country, but that was two years ago.
Do you want to learn in a manual or an automatic car?
Manual, please. My family's car is manual.
Our standard lessons are ninety minutes long. For beginners, we find that's better than an hour.
That's fine. Can the instructor pick me up?
Yes, from home or from work. Where would be best?
From my college, please. I finish classes at two.
Then Wednesday afternoons would work well. We have a space at half past two.
Great. How much does each lesson cost?
Forty pounds. But if you book ten lessons at once, you get one extra lesson free.
I'll think about that. Do I need to bring anything?
Yes, you must bring your provisional licence to the first lesson. The instructor has to check it before you drive.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A firefighter talks about a fire station open day.
script: Hi everyone. I'm Craig, one of the firefighters at Westside Fire Station, and I'd like to tell you about our open day next Saturday.
We hold the open day every year. People sometimes think it's to raise money, but the main purpose is to teach local families about fire safety in a fun way.
There's very little parking at the station itself, so please use the car park at the primary school next door. The head teacher has kindly agreed to that.
Children will be able to sit in the fire engine and try on helmets, all day long.
And every household from the local area that visits will receive a free smoke alarm. Our team can even fit it for you if you ask.
Now, the programme. The day starts at ten o'clock with a first aid workshop, where you can learn basic skills such as how to help someone who is choking.
At eleven thirty, we'll show you what happens when water is thrown onto a burning pan of oil, which is one of the most common causes of kitchen fires. It's quite dramatic.
Also at eleven thirty, children can try the hose challenge, aiming water at targets.
At one o'clock, there's a rescue demonstration, where we'll show how we cut people out of a crashed car.
At three o'clock, our search dogs will show how they find people trapped in collapsed buildings.
And also at three, just before we close, we'll hold the prize draw.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: What is the main purpose of the open day?
What can children do all day?

groups.instr: At what time does each event take place? Choose A, B, C or D. You may use any letter more than once.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: A student, Nora, discusses her lab report with her tutor, Dr Lin.
script: Hello Nora. Let's talk about your lab report on yeast.
Thanks. Just to remind you, the aim was to find out how temperature affects the rate of fermentation.
And you measured the volume of gas produced, which is carbon dioxide.
Yes. What surprised me was the result at fifty degrees. I expected the most gas, but there was almost none.
That's because the high temperature kills the yeast. You should explain that in your discussion.
OK. What did you think of my graph?
The type of graph is right, but you haven't labelled the axes. A reader can't tell what's being measured.
I'll fix that. When is the final version due?
Next Monday. Now, let's look at each section. Your introduction is clear, but you need references to support your background information.
The method is very well written. Someone else could easily repeat your experiment.
There are some errors in your calculations. Check the averages again.
It's too short. You need to explain your results in much more detail. Oh, and the risk assessment should be moved to the appendix.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: What was the aim of the experiment?
options: to see how temperature affects fermentation
There was little gas at 50 degrees.
The yeast did not react at all.

items.q: What does Dr Lin say about the graph?
When is the final report due?

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the history of Easter Island.
script: Today we're looking at Easter Island, one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth. It lies in the Pacific Ocean, about three thousand seven hundred kilometres from the coast of Chile.
The island was settled by Polynesian voyagers. Recent dating suggests that people arrived around 1200 AD, later than was once thought.

The island is famous for its giant stone statues, called moai. They were carved from volcanic rock in a quarry on the side of an extinct volcano. There are almost a thousand of them, and the largest weighs more than eighty tonnes.

How were they moved? For a long time, people assumed they were dragged lying down on wooden sledges. But experiments have shown that they could be 'walked' upright, by teams of people rocking them from side to side using ropes. This matches local stories that the statues walked to their places.

Easter Island has often been told as a story of environmental collapse. The island was once covered in palm forests, which disappeared, and some writers argued that islanders destroyed their own environment cutting trees to move statues. But recent research suggests that rats, which arrived with the first settlers, ate the palm seeds and played a major role in the loss of the forest.
The real catastrophe came after Europeans arrived in 1722. In the nineteenth century, slave raids and disease killed most of the population. By 1877, only one hundred and eleven islanders remained.
Today the population has recovered, and the islanders call their home by its own name: Rapa Nui.

passages.title: The Telescope in Orbit
paragraphs: On Earth, even the best telescopes must look through the atmosphere, which blurs and distorts the light from distant objects. In 1990, the Space Shuttle Discovery carried a telescope into orbit around 540 kilometres above the Earth, where it could observe the universe without this interference. It was named after Edwin Hubble, the American astronomer who showed in the 1920s that many galaxies exist beyond our own Milky Way.

The launch was quickly followed by embarrassment. The first images sent back by the Hubble Space Telescope were blurred. Engineers discovered that its main mirror had been ground to slightly the wrong shape. The error was tiny, around one-fiftieth of the thickness of a human hair, but it was enough to spoil the telescope's vision. The mistake had not been detected before launch because of a fault in the equipment used to test the mirror.

Fortunately, Hubble had been designed to be visited by astronauts. In 1993, a Space Shuttle crew installed corrective optics, effectively giving the telescope a pair of glasses. The results were spectacular. Over the following years, astronauts carried out a total of five servicing missions, replacing instruments, batteries and gyroscopes, with the last taking place in 2009.

Hubble has transformed our understanding of the universe. Its observations helped astronomers to estimate the age of the universe at around 13.8 billion years. In 1998, measurements of distant exploding stars, using Hubble and ground-based telescopes, showed that the expansion of the universe is speeding up rather than slowing down, a discovery that led to the idea of 'dark energy'.

Some of its most famous images were also among its simplest. In 1995, astronomers pointed Hubble at a tiny, apparently empty patch of sky for over ten days. The resulting picture, known as the Hubble Deep Field, revealed around 3,000 galaxies, some of them seen as they were billions of years ago.

Hubble is still operating, although some of its equipment is ageing. In 2021, its successor, the James Webb Space Telescope, was launched. Webb observes mainly infrared light and can see even further back in time, but astronomers regard the two telescopes as complementary, and Hubble remains in great demand.

passages.title: Listening to Whales
paragraphs: In 1967, the biologists Roger Payne and Scott McVay analysed recordings of humpback whales made by a navy engineer near Bermuda. They realised that the strange sounds were not random but formed long, repeated patterns, which they described as songs. In 1970, an album of the recordings, Songs of the Humpback Whale, became an unexpected bestseller. Hearing the haunting songs changed how many people thought about whales and helped to build public support for the campaign to end commercial whaling.

Humpback songs are remarkably complex. Only males sing, mainly during the breeding season, and each song consists of themes that are repeated in a fixed order, sometimes for hours. All the males in a population sing roughly the same song, but the song gradually changes over time. Researchers in Australia have even observed new songs spreading from one population to another across the South Pacific, like fashions spreading between countries.

Sperm whales communicate in a different way, using rapid series of clicks known as codas. Long-term studies in the Caribbean and the Pacific have shown that sperm whales live in clans, and that each clan uses its own set of codas, rather like a dialect. Whales appear to use these patterns to identify members of their own group.

New technology is allowing scientists to study whale communication in far greater detail. Project CETI, launched in 2020, uses underwater microphones and machine learning to analyse huge numbers of sperm whale clicks, with the ambitious aim of understanding what, if anything, they mean.

Whale communication faces a growing threat from human noise. Shipping produces low-frequency sound that travels long distances underwater and can mask whales' calls. Some whales respond by calling louder or more often. A remarkable natural experiment occurred after the attacks of 11 September 2001, when shipping in the Bay of Fundy in Canada was greatly reduced for several days. Researchers found that stress hormones in the local right whales fell during this quieter period.

Many scientists urge caution about claims that we will soon be able to 'talk to whales'. Whale communication evolved in a world very different from ours, and it may not resemble human language at all. Even if computers can identify patterns, understanding their meaning may remain beyond our reach. Nevertheless, listening carefully to whales has already changed the way we treat them, and may yet teach us much more.

passages.title: Are Phones Harming Teenagers?
paragraphs: Few questions in public life are debated as fiercely as whether smartphones and social media are damaging young people's mental health. In several countries, rates of anxiety and depression among teenagers, especially girls, began to rise in the early 2010s, around the time that smartphones became common. The psychologist Jonathan Haidt has argued that this is no coincidence: in his view, the move from a 'play-based childhood' to a 'phone-based childhood' is a major cause of the problem.

Other researchers are more cautious. They point out that most of the evidence is correlational: it shows that heavy social media users are more likely to report poor mental health, but it cannot show which causes which. Unhappy teenagers may spend more time online, rather than the other way round. In one widely discussed analysis, the researchers Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski found that the association between technology use and wellbeing was very small, comparable to the association with eating potatoes. In my view, it is fair to say that research has not proved that social media causes depression.

Nevertheless, there is good evidence of specific harms. Online bullying can follow young people home in a way that playground bullying could not. Using phones late at night is associated with shorter and poorer sleep, which itself affects mood and concentration. And in 2021, leaked internal research from a major social media company suggested that some teenage girls said the platform made them feel worse about their bodies.

It would be a mistake, however, to ignore the benefits. For many young people, social media is a way to maintain friendships, find information and express themselves creatively. For those who feel isolated, such as young people with rare illnesses or those who feel different from their peers, online communities can provide valuable support.

Governments have begun to act. In 2024, Australia passed a law banning children under 16 from having accounts on major social media platforms, placing the responsibility for enforcement on the companies. Many schools around the world have banned phones during the school day. It is too early to know how effective these measures will be.

I believe that the debate is often framed too simply, as a choice between banning phones and doing nothing. Age limits and school phone bans are reasonable, but the most important changes may concern the design of the platforms themselves. Features such as endless scrolling and constant notifications are designed to keep users online as long as possible. Companies should be required to change these designs for young users, rather than leaving parents and teenagers to resist them alone.

task1.text: The table below shows the number of mobile phone subscriptions per 100 people in five countries in 2000, 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The table shows the number of mobile phone subscriptions per 100 people in Bangladesh, India, Nigeria, the UK and the USA in 2000, 2010 and 2020.

Overall, mobile phone use increased dramatically in all five countries, especially in the three developing countries, which started from almost zero. By 2020, the differences between the countries had narrowed considerably.

In 2000, mobile phones were already common in the UK, with 74 subscriptions per 100 people, and fairly widespread in the USA, at 38. In Bangladesh, India and Nigeria, by contrast, the figures were below one per 100 people.

By 2010, the number of subscriptions had risen sharply everywhere. The UK had 123 per 100 people, meaning that many people had more than one subscription, while the figure for the USA reached 91. India, Nigeria and Bangladesh had between 45 and 61. Over the following decade, Bangladesh, Nigeria and the USA all passed or approached 100, reaching 105, 99 and 107 respectively, while India rose to 84. The UK figure, however, fell slightly to 118, although it remained the highest.

task2.text: Many older people find it difficult to use modern technology, such as smartphones and online banking. Some people think it is the responsibility of families to help them, while others believe governments should provide training. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: As more services move online, from banking to booking medical appointments, older people who are not confident with technology risk being left behind. There is disagreement about who should help them. In my view, families have an important role, but governments must also take responsibility, because the problem affects society as a whole.

Those who believe families should take the lead argue that relatives are best placed to help. Children and grandchildren know their elderly relatives' needs, can explain things patiently in a familiar way, and are usually available for repeated questions. Learning from a family member can also be less intimidating than attending a class with strangers. Moreover, such help strengthens relationships between generations.

On the other hand, not every older person has family nearby, and many relatives are too busy to provide regular support. Some older people live alone, and they are often the ones who most need online services. Furthermore, family members are not always skilled teachers, and they may simply do tasks for their relatives instead of teaching them. Since governments are moving public services online, it seems fair that they should ensure everyone can use them. Free courses in libraries and community centres, as well as telephone helplines, can reach people that families cannot.

In my opinion, the best approach combines both. Families should help where they can, but governments should provide free training and, importantly, keep non-digital options available, such as telephone and face-to-face services, for those who cannot or do not wish to go online.
In conclusion, although families can offer valuable personal support, I believe governments have the main responsibility to make sure that older people are not excluded by technology.

speaking.cue:
Describe an advertisement that you remember well.
You should say:
- what it was for
- where you saw it
- what happened in it
and explain why you remember it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about a television advertisement for a mobile phone company that was shown in Bangladesh during Eid a few years ago. Most phone adverts just show young people dancing or famous actors smiling, but this one was completely different. It told the story of an elderly father living alone in a village, whose son works in Dubai. The father is shown doing everyday things, feeding his chickens and going to the market, and you can see he's lonely. Then, at the end, his son surprises him with a video call on Eid morning, and you see the father's face light up as he sees his grandchildren for the first time. There was hardly any talking, just music, and only at the very end did the company's name appear. I saw it at home with my family, and I remember that my mother actually cried. I think I remember it so well because it focused on emotions rather than on the product. It reminded people that technology is really about connecting with the people we love, and it reflected something very real, since so many Bangladeshi families have members working abroad.
